messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: divergency fun
parts:
Hi!

My basic question is: Can I drop chains which show a divergency if I am quite sure that these chains failed to warmup appropriately?

The thing is, I just came across a model and data situation which required huge care to avoid those divergencies. The model is a hierarchical logistic regression and I had to scale things right, use NCP and start stan with adapt_delta=0.99 and a stepsize of 0.01. Under these very conservative settings I still get from time to time 1-4 divergencies.

I suspect that Stan did not succeed during warmup to find conservative enough sampling parameters for some of the chains. As a result some of the chains (but not all) suffer from divergencies. Is it OK to drop those chains in question from the results?

Are there other means to make Stan come up with ultra-conservative sampling parameters?

Another "solution" is often to rerun Stan with a different random seed.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] divergency fun
parts:
No.

Rarely does poor warmup lead to divergences — it almost always causes
the step size to drop to very small values at which point the sampler slows
to a crawl and you hit max treedepth warnings.

But more importantly, if you suspect that warmup is an issue than you can
easily inspect it by looking at the mass matrices (apparently only available
in CmdStan right now).  If they are the same for all chains then there is no
indication that anything when wrong, but if one chain has a mass matrix
with particularly small or large values _then_ you can be suspect of the
warmup procedure.  In that case you can tweak the warmup procedure
using the window length parameters described in the manual.

If you step back and analyze the posterior I bet you’ll find that the problem
is simpler than you have concluded.  In the non-centered parameterization
there are strong correlations between the population mean and population
standard deviation: when the population standard deviation is large the
mean can vary more, causing a tilt of the typical funnel geometry.  In particular,
if you plot the population mean vs the population standard deviation you’ll
see a skewed triangle with long corners when the standard deviation is large
and positive and the mean is large (either positive or negative).  It’s there 
that the divergences usually occur.

The simple answer is to tighten your priors a little bit.  Adding more regularization
to the population standard deviation is always helpful, but if you are weary of
that then you can try tightening the population mean prior a bit and that should
clean up the stray divergences quickly.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: divergency fun
parts:
Yeah currently get_adaptation_info in rstan just returns NULL, although Daniel just got it back up and running on the feature/refactor-stan-services branch in the RStan repo. 

Sebastian, in case you do try Daniel's branch you should be able to get the diagonal elements of the inverse mass matrix for each chain as a numeric vector (instead of embedded in strings) like this

library("stringr")
lapply(get_adaptation_info(fit), function(a) {
  x <- unlist(str_split(a, "mass matrix"))
  x <- str_extract_all(x[2], "\\(?[0-9,.]+\\)?")
  as.numeric(gsub(",","", unlist(x)))
})

That returns a list of vectors, one per chain. There's probably an easier way to do it, but that should work.

Jonah
